The World Bank’s USDC Plan Has a Problem Nobody Mentions
description:
Quick read Citi and Circle will explore USDC disbursements. No countries, corridors, volumes or dates disclosed. FundsChain already tracks spending, […]
The post The World Bank’s USDC Plan Has a Problem Nobody Mentions appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Quick read

  • Citi and Circle will explore USDC disbursements.
  • No countries, corridors, volumes or dates disclosed.
  • FundsChain already tracks spending, not USDC flows.
  • Nobody has named who converts USDC locally.

In its November 17 announcement, the World Bank Group said it will work with Citi and Circle to explore how regulated dollar stablecoins could sit alongside, or improve, the correspondent-banking system it uses to disburse funds today.

What the World Bank says faster money would buy

The pitch is about efficiency at scale. Development lenders face tight budgets and harder problems, the Bank argues, so even modest gains in payment cost and speed could free significant money for projects. President Ajay Banga made it concrete: faster, cheaper payments could mean clinics built on time and farmers paid before the harvest ends.

Each partner brings one piece. Citi supplies its existing links to banking rails, and its head of services, Shahmir Khaliq, described the goal as 24/7 capability that moves critical funds in real time across a network of more than 180 jurisdictions. Circle mints and settles USDC. Its chief executive, Jeremy Allaire, said funds should reach the people who need them with visibility into how they are used.

The first phase will run through intermediaries, in borrower countries that already support and permit digital assets, with other banks invited later. That is the full extent of the detail. The release names no country, corridor, payment volume, cost estimate or start date.

Real time describes the transfer. A clinic gets built on time when its contractor gets paid on time, and the bank-to-bank leg is only one stop on that route.

Where a project payment actually waits

World Bank money reaches projects in a handful of standard ways. The Bank can reimburse a borrower for spending it has already covered, advance funds into a designated account that the project draws down, pay a supplier directly at the borrower’s request, or back a letter of credit through a special commitment. Every route starts at the same gate. Someone has to show the expense qualifies.

Borrower institutions run that gate. The Bank’s financial-management framework places project payments inside national systems for budgeting, internal controls, accounting and audit. Swapping the settlement rail leaves every one of those checks where it was.

Lay the announcement over a single payment and it splits three ways. Two stages already have tools. One gets the new rail. Two get nothing named at all.

One project payment, five stages

1. Approval

Handled by borrower controls, Bank review and FundsChain.

Nov 17 adds: nothing

2. Bank-to-bank transfer

Handled by correspondent banks.

Nov 17 adds: a USDC rail

3. Local cash-out

Handled by the receiving bank and its FX desk.

Nov 17 adds: not specified

4. Supplier payment

Paid from a project account or directly by the Bank.

Nov 17 adds: not specified

5. Reconciliation

Handled by expenditure statements, audits and FundsChain.

Nov 17 adds: a visibility pledge

The two amber cards are the ones a supplier feels. Value can land at a receiving institution in seconds and then sit there while someone arranges conversion, credits the right account and clears compliance checks.

FundsChain already covers the paperwork

The World Bank already uses blockchain, just not to move money. Its FundsChain platform lets authorized parties trace project spending and tie each transaction to contracts and invoices. The November release puts its reach at more than 350 projects across 96 countries.

Read that figure carefully. It counts projects onboarded for tracking, and tells you nothing about how many would ever receive USDC.

FundsChain also shows what Allaire’s “visibility” would look like in practice. The platform’s September 2025 FAQ describes a private blockchain with access controls, where large files and sensitive data stay off-chain and only link back to it. Project parties see more. The public does not get a window into every invoice.

A separate FundsChain thread runs in parallel. A July 2 update described a six-month FundsChain Evolution pilot in Ethiopia that tests programmable rules over how funds move. That work sets conditions on spending, while the Citi-Circle project concerns the rail underneath. The November release does not name Ethiopia as a USDC participant.

Nobody has named the local exit

USDC is a dollar token. A road contractor in a borrowing country often invoices in local currency, pays local wages and banks with a local lender.

Someone has to turn USDC into spendable local money and credit the right account, and the release does not say who. Citi’s network of more than 180 jurisdictions makes it an obvious candidate. Neither partner has said Citi will take that role, what it would charge or what hours it would keep.

Circle’s own redemption terms show why the answer changes the outcome. Settlement timing depends on the transaction method and the banking rails involved, and Circle offers free Standard redemptions next to fee-bearing Express ones. Speed can carry a price. Those are Circle’s public terms, though, not whatever the three partners negotiate for this program.

Local banks also have to want the business. Coindoo’s look at bank stablecoin plans found most banks preparing stablecoin services while few expect broad demand. In a small borrower market, that raises a blunt question: will any local lender take on the conversion? Regulation narrows the field before demand even comes up. The pilot only covers countries that already permit digital assets. Coindoo’s coverage of Singapore’s digital-money initiative, which also counts the World Bank Group among its participants, shows how much legal groundwork has to happen before systems can connect at all.

READ MORE:

Ethereum’s Next Upgrade Could Let Callers Skip Payments

What a fair test against bank wires looks like

The G20 already set the yardstick. Its cross-border payment targets for 2027 measure speed by when recipients can use the funds, aiming for 75% of payments to reach that point within one hour of initiation. Banks reaching each other faster doesn’t count until the money lands.

The incumbent route isn’t standing still either. The Financial Stability Board’s 2025 progress report found that global wholesale cross-border payments have become faster. That is the segment a USDC rail would compete in.

A credible trial would run matched payments through one corridor, with the same amount, the same destination currency and the same recipient requirements. Then it would publish three numbers: the time from instruction to spendable funds, what the supplier receives after every charge including conversion, and the staff hours spent reconciling each payment.

Liquidity needs its own line. Projects that run on advances keep cash parked in designated accounts before they spend it. If a faster route lets the Bank advance less, the saving equals what it costs to fund that smaller balance, not the balance itself. Count the balance instead and “significant resources” grows on paper only.

The next useful disclosure would be small and specific: one named corridor, the local partner that cashes USDC out, and an all-in cost set against the correspondent-banking route it replaces. Until then, Banga’s on-time clinic is a promise nobody can check.

title: Solana Price Rebounds Toward $80 As Buyers Return — Can SOL Break Its Downtrend?
description: Solana price is showing renewed signs of strength after a difficult period for the cryptocurrency market, with buyers pushing SOL back toward $75 following a sharp decline below $70 earlier this week. The recovery has raised an important question among traders: could Solana be preparing for a breakout toward $80, or is the latest move […]
fullContent:
Solana price is showing renewed signs of strength after a difficult period for the cryptocurrency market, with buyers pushing SOL back toward $75 following a sharp decline below $70 earlier this week. The recovery has raised an important question among traders: could Solana be preparing for a breakout toward $80, or is the latest move simply a temporary rebound?

The price recovery comes as Solana continues expanding its infrastructure, with recent network developments strengthening its position in decentralized finance and institutional blockchain applications.

According to historical market data, SOL climbed from approximately $71.55 at the beginning of November 17 to $75.13 by the end of the session, representing a gain of around 5%.

However, the cryptocurrency remains considerably below its early-November levels, making the next few trading sessions particularly important.

Solana Price Recovery Gains Momentum As Buyers Defend $70

Solana’s latest recovery follows several days of intense selling pressure that pushed the cryptocurrency to a November 15 low near $67.79.

The decline came after SOL traded above $90 earlier this month, highlighting the extent of the recent correction.

Nevertheless, buyers returned as prices approached the $68–$70 region, helping Solana stabilize and eventually recover above $75.

The November 17 session recorded approximately $3.29 billion in trading volume, suggesting that the recovery was accompanied by substantial market participation.

While this figure was slightly below the previous session’s $3.43 billion, the price advance indicates that buying pressure was sufficient to overcome selling activity during the rebound.

For traders, the most encouraging development is Solana’s ability to establish a higher price following the recent market low.

However, one strong session does not automatically confirm a broader trend reversal.

Solana Faces Its First Major Test Near $75–$80

The next important challenge for Solana is whether buyers can sustain the recovery beyond the recent trading range.

SOL reached approximately $75.38 during the November 17 session before encountering resistance.

A sustained move above this level could open the door toward $78.40, followed by the psychologically important $80 resistance area.

These levels are particularly relevant because Solana previously traded above $80 before the latest correction accelerated.

If buyers successfully reclaim $80, market participants could begin watching the $83–$85 region, where SOL traded earlier in November.

However, failure to maintain momentum above $75 could encourage another test of nearby support.

The $71–$72 area represents the first important defensive region, while $68 remains a deeper support level associated with the November 15 low.

A breakdown below that level would weaken the short-term recovery scenario.

Solana’s Network Developments Add Another Dimension To The Recovery

Beyond technical indicators, Solana’s recent infrastructure improvements provide an additional reason to monitor the cryptocurrency.

As Bitcoinist reported, the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation recently outlined plans to connect its tokenization infrastructure to Solana.

The development could eventually bring additional traditional financial assets onto the blockchain, strengthening its role in institutional settlement and tokenized securities.

Meanwhile, Solana has officially retired its long-standing mainnet beta designation, introducing a new protocol versioning system intended to simplify coordination across validator implementations.

These developments demonstrate that network expansion is continuing even as cryptocurrency prices experience substantial volatility.

However, stronger blockchain infrastructure does not automatically translate into immediate demand for SOL.

The relationship between adoption, network activity, and token valuation will remain an important consideration for investors.

Can Solana Price Reach $80 Before The Next Major Correction?

Solana’s recent rebound has improved the short-term technical picture, but confirmation remains essential.

We believe the $75–$80 region will be particularly important in determining whether the latest recovery can develop into a more sustained advance.

A decisive breakout above $75.38, supported by stronger trading activity, would improve the likelihood of a move toward $78.40 and eventually $80.

Conversely, another rejection near resistance could leave SOL vulnerable to renewed selling pressure.

The broader market environment also remains influential, particularly as Bitcoin continues navigating its own important support levels.

For now, Solana has demonstrated that buyers remain active despite the recent correction. Whether that demand is strong enough to establish a lasting reversal will depend on how the cryptocurrency performs around its next major resistance levels.

fullContent:
November 18th, 2026 – Singapore, Singapore

PancakeSwap today announced that it has rebranded as Pancake.

The new name reflects how far the platform has grown since launch, from a single-chain token swap into a multichain liquidity hub where users can trade, earn and build.

Pancake launched in 2020 on one chain, known for one thing: swapping tokens. Over six years, it expanded to 11+ chains including BNB Chain, Base, Robinhood Chain, Arbitrum, Solana and Ethereum, and added products well beyond swaps. More than 208 million users have traded over $4.4 trillion on the platform.

Today, Pancake brings three groups of products together in one place:

  • Trade: Swap any token, go long or short with Perps or buy tokenized stocks and ETFs 24/7 on Stock Terminal, weekends included. The Pancake Aggregator routes each trade to the best available price across the market.
  • Earn: Stake CAKE in Syrup Pools or use Dual Investment to set a target price and earn yield while waiting for it.
  • Build: Developers can add custom features to Pancake’s liquidity pools through Infinity hooks or integrate the Pancake Aggregator directly into their own apps.

Upcoming Mobile App Launch

A new name is only the first course. In the coming weeks, Pancake will launch its mobile app, built to be the best way to trade DeFi from your pocket: the full Pancake stack, one tap away, around the clock. Early users can expect a few surprises along the way so stay tuned.

About Pancake

Pancake (formerly PancakeSwap) is a multichain liquidity hub live across 11+ chains. Users can swap, trade perpetuals and tokenized stocks, and earn with Syrup Pools and Dual Investment. Builders can tap Pancake’s liquidity through Infinity, its DEX aggregator and B2B integrations. Launched in 2020, Pancake has processed over $4.4 trillion in trading volume. Users can learn more at https://pancake.xyz/.

title: Aave App Launches on TRON, Bringing USDT Deposits to Mobile Users on Android and iOS
description: Geneva, Switzerland –  TRON DAO, the community-governed DAO dedicated to accelerating the decentralization of the internet through blockchain technology and decentralized applications (dApps), today announced that the Aave App, a high-yield savings mobile app developed and managed by Aave Labs, will add support for USDT (TRC-20) deposits on the TRON network as it expands to Android following its initial launch on iOS.   The launch combines Android’s global reach with TRON’s leading role in the stablecoin ecosystem, expanding mobile access to onchain savings opportunities that are not accessible on traditional savings apps. With support for USDT on TRON, eligible users in supported jurisdictions can now deposit USDT on TRON and start earning yield on their savings.   Android’s extensive global footprint offers a significant distribution opportunity for digital asset applications, particularly in markets where stablecoins are used for payments, remittances, and savings. TRON provides an established infrastructure for this opportunity, with more than $94 billion in circulating USDT, the largest circulating supply of Tether’s dollar-pegged stablecoin among blockchain networks. TRON also supports a broad range of stablecoin use cases, including payments, cross-border transfers, and digital asset transactions.   Aave is building the World’s Savings App, a simple, globally accessible tool designed to help people grow and manage their savings, with a delightful design experience on the surface and powerful onchain finance infrastructure working under the hood. fullContent:
Bitcoin price is still under pressure, trading below $65,000. The latest institutional development, however, comes from the stablecoin market. The World Bank Group is exploring Circle’s USDC with Citi to move development funds through blockchain-based payment infrastructure.

The 82-year-old institution wants to determine if regulated stablecoins can make international disbursements faster, cheaper, and more transparent. Its proposed arrangement combines Circle’s USDC settlement infrastructure with Citi’s established banking connections. The initiative builds on FundsChain, the World Bank’s existing blockchain platform covering more than 350 projects across 96 countries.

The announcement arrives as Bitcoin price struggles to recover from a sharp market correction. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded another $239.9 million in net outflows yesterday. Yet institutional adoption of blockchain-based dollar payments continues to expand.

Now, will the growing movement of dollars onto blockchain rails eventually provide another source of liquidity for Bitcoin?

Market Cap

DISCOVER: 15+ Best Crypto IPO to Watch in 2026

World Bank Turns to Circle’s USDC for Global Payments

The World Bank Group announced its exploration last night, bringing together two major financial infrastructure providers. Circle will provide the stablecoin infrastructure to mint and settle funds in USDC. Citi will connect those transactions with established correspondent banking networks.

CONFIRMED: The World Bank Group is exploring CRYPTO dollars to pay out its funds, using Circle's $USDC with Citi.

The 82-year-old lender will test whether USDC can move development money faster and cheaper than today's bank-to-bank transfers.

Its blockchain platform FundsChain… pic.twitter.com/Yz9bGObXQ8

— Coin Bureau (@coinbureau) November 18, 2026

The objective is to improve how development financing reaches governments, businesses, and local projects. Traditional international payments often involve multiple banking intermediaries, processing windows, and settlement delays. Blockchain-based settlement could reduce some of these obstacles through faster transaction processing.

Citi says its network connects clients across more than 180 jurisdictions. The bank wants to deliver 24/7 payment capabilities, allowing critical funds to move in real time. Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire also described development finance as an important application for internet-native money.

“Circle is building the infrastructure for an internet-native financial system, and development finance is one of its most important applications.” – Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire

The initiative builds on FundsChain, which already provides transparency across the World Bank’s development projects. Its digital ledgers allow participating parties to track how project funds are used. The platform currently covers more than 350 projects across 96 countries.

The potential scale is considerable. The World Bank Group delivered $123.5 billion in loans, grants, equity investments, and guarantees during fiscal 2026. Its latest exploration could eventually introduce stablecoin settlement into a substantial institutional financial network.

However, the initial exploration will involve borrower countries where digital assets are permitted. The World Bank also plans an intermediated and interoperable payment model, connecting blockchain infrastructure with conventional banking systems.

DISCOVER: 15+ Upcoming Coinbase Listings to Watch in 2026

Bitcoin Price Could Benefit From Expanding Dollar Liquidity

USDC has become one of the most important dollar-denominated assets circulating across blockchain networks. Circle reported an average USDC circulation of $73.3 billion during Q3 2026. Its on-chain transaction volume reached $13.9 trillion, representing 49% annual growth.

Circle’s latest earnings presentation also showed USDC accounting for 79% of stablecoin transaction volume. That figure compares with its 27% share of stablecoin supply. The difference highlights how frequently USDC moves across blockchain-based financial applications.

This matters because stablecoins provide much of the dollar liquidity used throughout crypto markets. Traders use USDC to enter positions, move capital between exchanges, and settle transactions. Greater institutional adoption could expand the infrastructure supporting these activities.

Bitcoin remains the largest crypto and a major destination for digital asset capital. More accessible stablecoin infrastructure could make it easier for institutions and market participants to move dollars into crypto markets. That creates a potential second-order benefit for Bitcoin price and liquidity.

The timing is interesting given the current market conditions. Bitcoin price is hovering below $65,000, while US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $239.9 million in withdrawals on November 17. BlackRock’s IBIT accounted for $209.5 million of those outflows.

The contrast between weakening Bitcoin demand and expanding institutional stablecoin infrastructure raises an interesting question. Could the next phase of cryptocurrency liquidity come from traditional financial institutions moving dollars onto blockchain rails?

fullContent:
Billionaire Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway has sold most of its Capital One (COF) stake in just two quarters.

The conglomerate held 1,150,000 Capital One (COF) shares on September 30th, down from 7,150,000 on March 31st, reports Yahoo Finance.

Berkshire cut the stake to 3,000,000 COF shares in the second quarter, then to 1,150,000 in the third.

Over six months, 6,000,000 COF shares were sold, or 83.9% of the position.

The firm unloaded 1,850,000 COF shares in the third quarter, which were worth about $357 million at the September 30th price of $193.07.

The remaining shares were worth about $222 million, or 0.07% of the firm’s $304.20 billion portfolio, according to Berkshire’s latest 13F filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

Berkshire also trimmed Bank of America (BAC) by 5.7% in the third quarter to 455,860,908 BAC shares, a sale worth about $1.5 billion.

Meanwhile, the conglomerate’s American Express (AXP) stake did not change.

The 13F filing shows holdings as of September 30th and says nothing about trades since then.

Berkshire filed it on Monday, November 16th.

Greg Abel has run Berkshire as chief executive since the start of 2026, after Warren Buffett stepped down at the end of 2025.

The filing does not say who made each trade.

Capital One is a major US credit card issuer and bank.

title: US Senators Question SEC Tokenized-Stock Exemption Over Wallet Transfers and Investor Protection
description: Four Democratic US senators have pressed the Securities and Exchange Commission for answers about how its new approach to tokenized stock trading will protect investors.
fullContent:
TL;DR

  • Four Democratic senators challenged the SEC’s tokenized-stock trading exemption in a new letter.
  • Their concerns include wallet-to-wallet transfers, AML checks, pricing and issuer protections.
  • The letter seeks clarification and oversight; it does not itself revoke the exemption.

Four Democratic US senators have pressed the Securities and Exchange Commission for answers about how its new approach to tokenized stock trading will protect investors and prevent illicit transfers. Their November 16 letter, reported by The Block, takes aim at gaps they see in the SEC’s five-year innovation exemption for certain trading venues. The development is an oversight challenge, not a court ruling or a notice that the exemption has been cancelled. It goes to a central difficulty for tokenized securities: a regulated purchase can become a blockchain transfer to another address.

What the exemption is intended to enable

The SEC introduced its approach in September, allowing qualifying tokenized-securities venues to operate under a defined exemption from some ordinary exchange-registration requirements. The aim is to permit experimentation with trading stocks in token form while the agency assesses a new market structure. A token representing a security still raises questions about ownership, trading rules and investor rights. The exemptions and their precise conditions matter more than a general statement that securities have moved on-chain. Not every blockchain token, broker or venue automatically qualifies for the same regulatory treatment.

The lawmakers’ main concern

Senators Angela Alsobrooks, Ruben Gallego, Mark Warner and Catherine Cortez Masto reportedly told SEC Chair Paul Atkins that the framework lacks sufficiently specific safeguards around know-your-customer and anti-money-laundering procedures. A buyer verified by a regulated venue might later transfer a token to a wallet whose controller has not undergone the same checks. This problem is not solved merely by verifying the identity of the first purchaser. The letter asks how secondary transfers and the reach of compliance obligations would be managed once tokens circulate beyond the initial venue.

For related context, see our earlier report on Hong Kong's developing licensing rules.

Investor pricing and issuer rights also feature

The senators raised concerns about retail-investor protections and pricing, and reportedly asked whether companies could opt out of having their shares tokenized. Those questions are distinct from financial-crime screening. A token that references equity needs a clear relationship to the rights and obligations of the underlying security, as well as fair information about execution and ownership. If an issuer’s wishes, the investor’s expectations and the platform’s legal structure do not line up, technical transferability alone cannot resolve the conflict. Policymakers must address those issues in enforceable terms.

What happens next

The lawmakers asked the SEC to explain its approach and urged a transparent rulemaking process for changes in the regulatory treatment of tokenized securities. Such a letter can affect oversight and public debate, especially as control of congressional committees changes, but it is not itself binding legislation. Venues exploring tokenized equities should continue to follow the actual exemption terms and any subsequent SEC guidance. The next concrete milestones are the agency’s response, proposed revisions if any, and how early trading models implement identity, custody and transfer restrictions.

A workable compromise, if one emerges, may turn on which transfers are allowed after a regulated initial sale. Some token designs can restrict transfers to approved addresses, while others rely on venue-level checks or additional intermediaries. Each model gives up something different in portability, privacy or market openness. The senators' concerns therefore reach beyond rhetorical support for or opposition to blockchains: they ask what compliance guarantees exist when a security is represented by a programmable token that can move outside its original trading environment.

For related context, see our earlier report on new institutional crypto-custody arrangements.

Tokenization can change how securities move, but it does not automatically settle which rules should accompany them. The dispute now concerns the design of that regulatory perimeter, with no basis to describe the senators’ letter as an immediate prohibition on tokenized stocks.

Reporting sources: The Block report of four senators’ letter

Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

title: Ethereum’s Next Upgrade Could Let Callers Skip Payments
description:
Key Takeaways Caller gas limits can skip a 2.5% payment OP Stack withdrawals failed at the estimated gas EF estimate: […]
The post Ethereum’s Next Upgrade Could Let Callers Skip Payments appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Caller gas limits can skip a 2.5% payment
  • OP Stack withdrawals failed at the estimated gas
  • EF estimate: 10,000–15,000 of 90 million contracts
  • Core developers weigh EIP-8037/8038 on November 19

The findings come from tests of EIP-8037 and EIP-8038, two gas-repricing proposals that led AllCoreDevs to pause the Hoodi testnet fork, according to the Ethereum Foundation’s November 6 update.

A Withdrawal That Pays Everyone but One

The clearest case comes from a proof-of-concept repository published under the GitHub account mejango and cited in the developer discussion. Its vault sends 2.5% of each withdrawal to a separate component contract inside a try block. If that payment reverts, the vault keeps the share and the user is paid anyway, a common way to stop one broken component from freezing every withdrawal.

The author ran the same call at gas limits from 30,000 to 900,000 using eth_simulateV1 on public RPC endpoints, once against Ethereum mainnet and once against Sepolia, which the repository says already applies Glamsterdam gas rules. Nothing was deployed. On mainnet, every limit either reverted the whole withdrawal or paid the component. Under Glamsterdam rules, a band roughly 112,000 gas wide completed the withdrawal and skipped the payment.

These are the author’s simulations. Coindoo has not reproduced them, and they do not describe an exploit of a live contract.

The Caller Chooses Which Outcome Happens

The outer gas limit is set by whoever calls the withdrawal. According to the repository, that turns the band into a lever: a caller can pick a limit inside it on purpose, making the component payment fail while the withdrawal itself goes through.

The vault has no way to respond. Its contracts are immutable, so logic written to tolerate a broken component now also tolerates a deliberately underfunded one. Under current mainnet rules the same attempt fails, because a limit too low to fund the component also leaves too little gas to finish, and the whole transaction reverts.

Why the Payment Fails but the Fallback Survives

Two proposals produce that result together. EIP-8038 raises the gas cost of reading and writing state, so a budget that used to cover the component’s work can now run out sooner. EIP-8037 separates the cost of creating new state from ordinary execution gas and raises it. Coindoo has covered what that means for onboarding costs.

The second change is what keeps the fallback alive. ChainSecurity’s October 13 analysis explains that state-creation charges are drawn from a separate pool that is restored when a call fails, and that a failed call’s state charges paid from regular gas go back to its caller. A contract can therefore have more gas left after a failure than it would today.

ChainSecurity’s worked example uses a write to a fresh storage slot. Under current rules it costs 22,100 gas, so a failure handler with about 15,000 gas left runs out and the transaction reverts. Under the reviewed Glamsterdam specification, the same write costs 12,100 execution gas, while a 97,920-gas state charge comes from the separate pool, leaving room for the write and a short continuation. The write is not cheaper overall; a different pool pays for the expensive part.

The vault scenario needs both effects: the component’s call fails earlier because work costs more, and the vault’s fallback completes because it no longer runs out of gas. A contract that counted on running out of gas to force a rollback can end in a different state. ChainSecurity limits that conclusion to specific call patterns, and most findings reported so far stem from the cost increases rather than the separate pool, according to the summary of the November 16 testing call.

READ MORE:

Grayscale Reveals ‘Compelling Entry Points’ but Data Says No

When the Default Gas Estimate Lands in the Gap

A higher fee per unit of gas changes nothing here, because price does not add units to an internal call. A higher gas limit does help in the vault example, since larger limits pay the component, but only when the software setting the limit chooses a large enough number. The repository’s second test shows what happens when it uses the standard estimate.

That test models an OP Stack withdrawal being finalized on Ethereum, using the real OptimismPortal2 and L1CrossDomainMessenger contracts. The message being delivered requests a fixed 375,000 gas. On mainnet, finalizing at the eth_estimateGas result of 931,416 delivered the message. Under Glamsterdam rules on Sepolia, finalizing at the estimate of 1,517,344 succeeded, but the messenger recorded the delivery as failed and the funds were not credited. Doubling the limit delivered it.

The repository presents that estimate as the one a wallet or relayer would send, so the user would have done nothing unusual. Recovery remains possible because the messenger lets anyone replay a failed message, but it takes a third, manual transaction and another gas payment. The two runs also used different messenger versions, 2.11.1 on mainnet and 2.13.0 on Sepolia, a difference the comparison does not isolate.

The two gas sweeps side by side

Vault withdrawal – current mainnet rules

  • 30,000–106,000: whole withdrawal reverts
  • 108,000–898,000: component paid

Vault withdrawal – Glamsterdam rules

  • 30,000–180,000: whole withdrawal reverts
  • 182,000–294,000: withdrawal succeeds, payment skipped
  • 296,000: reverts
  • 298,000–898,000: component paid

OP Stack finalization – mainnet

  • 400,000–900,000: reverts, retry later
  • 925,000–10,000,000: message delivered

OP Stack finalization – Glamsterdam rules

  • 400,000–1,000,000: reverts
  • 1,025,000–1,600,000: finalized, delivery recorded as failed
  • 1,625,000–10,000,000: message delivered

Glamsterdam results were simulated on Sepolia. OP Stack runs were pinned to a single L1 block.

What a Success Receipt Does Not Show

In both tests, the transaction receipt reports success. A receipt’s status covers only the outer call. It says nothing about whether a call caught inside a try block, or a message handed to a bridge messenger, did what it was meant to do.

Confirming that means checking the specific evidence: a balance change or event from the component in the vault case and, for OP Stack withdrawals, whether the messenger emitted RelayedMessage or FailedRelayedMessage. A bridge interface that marks a withdrawal “finalized” from the receipt alone can show a user a completed withdrawal before any funds arrive.

10,000-15,000 Contracts, and Who Can Fix Them

At the November 16 testing call, the Ethereum Foundation’s Marius estimated that around 10,000–15,000 out of roughly 90 million contracts would be affected, according to the meeting’s auto-generated summary. The summary does not explain how that figure, or a separate value-at-risk estimate of “a few hundred thousand dollars,” was produced. A contract count is not an application count, and an affected contract does not necessarily put funds at risk.

Auditors brought their own tallies to the same call. ChainSecurity reported 152 findings, rising to 200 when combined with the Foundation’s internal search. The summary describes most findings as easy to mitigate, with some requiring contract upgrades or redeployment.

Who can apply a fix depends on where the outdated gas assumption sits:

  • Wallets and RPC providers can change how they estimate gas, the layer behind the OP Stack result.
  • Applications with adjustable gas settings can raise those values and retest them.
  • Upgradeable contracts can ship a new implementation, usually after a governance vote.
  • Immutable contracts cannot be patched. Their options are a supported retry, an external workaround, moving users to a replacement contract, or a change to the protocol rules themselves.

That last group is why the issue sits with core developers rather than app teams alone, a compatibility question Coindoo examined in its earlier look at how the upgrade could change old contracts. The testing-call summary also assigns follow-up work with affected app teams, L2s and OP Stack chains, including testnet replays to find contracts not yet identified.

What the November 19 Call Can Settle

Core developers take up the findings at the November 19 execution-layer call. The Foundation says no decision is pre-committed for that meeting, while the testing-call summary lists deciding whether to proceed with EIP-8037 and EIP-8038 as the action item.

Options raised on November 16 included proceeding as planned, dropping the proposal, waiting for contract-size limit increases, and delaying. Those favouring the current plan pointed to the post-quantum roadmap, and one developer warned that dropping the proposal would prevent large contracts from being deployed. The Foundation’s update adds that several specification revisions are being prototyped, each documented for the problems it fixes and the other invariants it could break.

Hoodi stays unforked until that is resolved. The gas bands above describe the proposal as tested, and any revision to the specifications would change the rules those simulations ran against.

title: Binance Hack-Linked Wallet Moves 34,279 ETH, but Investigators See No Confirmed Sale
description: A wallet linked by blockchain investigators to the October 29 Binance breach has transferred 34,279.66 ETH to three newly created addresses, ending a period of.
fullContent:
TL;DR

  • Investigators tracked 34,279.66 ETH from a Binance hack-linked address to three new wallets.
  • The movement was worth roughly $63 million at the reported market price.
  • No verified exchange deposit or executed sale had been established in the initial reports.

A wallet linked by blockchain investigators to the October 29 Binance breach has transferred 34,279.66 ETH to three newly created addresses, ending a period of inactivity. The ether was worth roughly $63 million at prices used in Tuesday’s reporting. That is a significant movement of suspected stolen funds, but a wallet transfer is not automatically a sale, a successful laundering step or proof that the recipient controls are independent of the sender. Investigators had not identified the new addresses as exchanges at the time of their initial reports.

The new transactions are visible on-chain

Monitoring groups MistTrack and Solid Intel reported the transfers on November 17. MistTrack described three movements of approximately 12,000 ETH, 12,000 ETH and 10,279.66 ETH. The receiving wallets were newly created, and the monitored funds had not moved again when the analysts published their findings. Public transaction records make it possible to trace the amounts and destinations, but they do not disclose the human operator behind each address. The link to the earlier breach rests on investigators’ attribution of the sending wallet, not a label embedded in the blockchain itself.

The wider breach remains unresolved

The October attack involved vastly larger losses than Tuesday’s movement. US investigators attributed the incident to a North Korean hacking group, and authorities have announced substantial asset restraints and seizures. Blockchain intelligence firms have also tracked funds moved through different assets and protocols. These parallel developments should not be added together casually, because frozen, seized, recovered and still-controlled amounts describe different legal and operational states. The fresh ETH transfers are one piece of a complex post-incident trail rather than an update to the full net-loss number.

For related context, see our earlier report on Coinbase's custody and security precautions.

Movement does not establish selling pressure

Crypto trading commentary sometimes treats any transfer from an exploit-linked wallet as preparation to dump tokens. That can happen, but the evidence here does not yet establish a market sale. Transfers may consolidate funds, redistribute control or precede another operation. Until an address is linked to a trading venue, bridge, mixer or other service, the immediate observable fact is the destination change. Even a later exchange deposit would need careful interpretation: deposits are not identical to executed sell orders. Reporting should preserve those steps rather than collapsing them into one dramatic conclusion.

Why transparency helps, and where it stops

Ethereum’s public ledger lets investigators monitor known addresses and alert service providers if assets reappear at identifiable points. Token issuers, exchanges and law enforcement may each have different powers depending on the assets and jurisdictions involved. Native ETH cannot simply be frozen by an issuer in the way some centrally administered tokens can. That difference complicates recovery when funds leave services that can intervene. The next useful evidence will be further movements, identification of services receiving the funds and official updates to the case.

Investigators can improve attribution confidence by comparing the sequence, amounts and transaction timing with addresses already associated with the incident. Yet public labels can be incomplete, and a newly created wallet may simply be another address controlled by the same actor. Readers should resist claims that funds have reached a criminal group, a particular country or a cash-out desk unless that identification is supported by additional evidence. Future investigative notices should specify their degree of confidence and distinguish observed transfers from hypotheses about their purpose.

For related context, see our earlier report on the Unocoin wallet compromise.

The latest transfer warrants close monitoring, but it should not be reported as the disposal of $63 million in stolen ether without further proof. The distinction between observable transactions and inferred intent is especially important in a security incident of this scale.

Reporting sources: CoinDesk report of MistTrack and Solid Intel monitoring · MistTrack transfer report

title: Grayscale Says November Crypto Slump Reflects Stablecoin Exits and Tech-Sector Stress
description: Grayscale’s latest market note offers a two-part explanation for the sharp decline in crypto prices: money moving out of stablecoins and pressure spilling over from.
fullContent:
TL;DR

  • Grayscale links crypto weakness to stablecoin off-ramping and pressure in AI-related equities.
  • Its analysis also highlights moving-average signals and leverage as possible amplifiers.
  • Its claim that prices offer attractive entry points is a manager’s opinion, not an established market outcome.

Grayscale’s latest market note offers a two-part explanation for the sharp decline in crypto prices: money moving out of stablecoins and pressure spilling over from technology equities. Head of research Zach Pandl argues that fundamental adoption trends remain intact, even while Bitcoin and other large assets struggle. That is the assessment of an asset manager with a commercial interest in digital assets, not a settled finding that the sell-off is over. Its value lies in examining the mechanisms rather than repeating the optimistic conclusion as fact.

Stablecoin supply is one signal

The November 16 research note points to accelerating withdrawals from stablecoins after the late-October Binance security incident. When investors redeem dollar-backed tokens for bank deposits, the supply of on-chain dollars can contract. That may reduce the liquidity available for trading and collateral, although it does not mean each redeemed dollar was about to buy Bitcoin. Other drivers can change supply, including arbitrage and issuer operations. Grayscale views off-ramping as one contributing factor to the November weakness. Confirming its influence requires tracking issuance, redemptions and market activity across venues.

AI-related equities may transmit risk

The firm also identifies pressure in Nvidia and other AI-linked stocks as a possible source of portfolio de-risking. Investors holding growth technology and crypto exposure may sell both when financing conditions worsen or their risk limits tighten. There is a further link through physical infrastructure: some Bitcoin mining firms are developing high-performance computing services for AI operators. Those connections do not make Bitcoin a direct claim on AI company earnings. They suggest overlapping investors and capital requirements through which stress can travel across otherwise different sectors.

For related context, see our earlier report on stablecoin supply contraction.

Technical selling can amplify the move

Grayscale notes that Bitcoin fell below its 200-day moving average on November 12, a level followed by some trend-oriented trading strategies. Leveraged positions and thinner weekend order books can make subsequent price moves more abrupt. Those mechanisms may amplify a decline without identifying a single fundamental cause. Importantly, technical signals are not universal commands: different funds use different models and time horizons, and a moving-average breach does not determine the market’s next direction. The research describes a chain of plausible forces, not a proven one-factor explanation.

What the bullish argument leaves open

Grayscale believes medium- and long-term investors may find current valuations attractive because institutional stablecoin and tokenization activity continues to develop. The note also acknowledges inflation, interest-rate uncertainty and geopolitical risk. Those headwinds could persist longer than optimistic scenarios assume. Readers should distinguish the factual observation of a significant drawdown from the manager’s valuation judgment. ETF flows, stablecoin supplies and changes in rates can help test the thesis, but none offers a reliable standalone timing signal.

Another test of the explanation is whether on-chain capital actually returns when equity-market stress eases. A rebound in technology shares accompanied by ongoing stablecoin redemptions would suggest the factors are not moving in lockstep. In contrast, renewed stablecoin issuance without a broader Bitcoin recovery would show that liquidity availability alone is insufficient. Such cross-checks are more informative than assigning every daily price move to the same narrative. They also allow readers to separate Grayscale's interpretation from the specific market data used to support it.

For related context, see our earlier report on recent bitcoin ETF outflows.

The report provides a framework for thinking about November’s crypto decline, not proof that prices have bottomed. Its strongest contribution is highlighting how stablecoin redemptions, shared growth-stock positioning and leveraged market structure can interact during a difficult month.

Reporting sources: Grayscale November 16 research note

title: Cypherpunk Reports 8,967 ZEC Mined as Zcash Treasury Nears 342,000 Tokens
description: Publicly traded Cypherpunk Technologies has reported the first results from its Zcash mining operation, producing 8,967.29 ZEC in just 44 days. The company says those.
fullContent:
TL;DR

  • Cypherpunk reported mining 8,967.29 ZEC during its first 44 operating days.
  • Its treasury reached about 341,859 ZEC after mining and purchases.
  • Operating earnings should be distinguished from large unrealized token-valuation gains.

Publicly traded Cypherpunk Technologies has reported the first results from its Zcash mining operation, producing 8,967.29 ZEC in just 44 days. The company says those tokens represented approximately $9.9 million of mining revenue in the third quarter, while its treasury later grew to about 341,859 ZEC through purchases and continued production. The figures are impressive in isolation. But investors need to separate operating earnings from accounting gains on an appreciated token reserve, especially after ZEC’s volatile price action.

Mining began only in August

Cypherpunk’s November 16 filing says the mining fleet began operation on August 18 and delivered about 95% uptime through September 30. The company reported revenue corresponding to 8,967.29 ZEC, with a stated average cost of mining revenue of approximately $104 per token before depreciation. Once depreciation of equipment is included, the company reported a higher per-token cost near $237. The distinction is crucial when comparing mining economics across companies because machines lose value over time even if their near-term power and hosting costs look low.

The treasury is larger than the quarter’s production

Cypherpunk says holdings reached around 341,858.75 ZEC after adding October mining output and recent market purchases, equivalent to roughly 2% of the circulating supply at its reporting date. Its strategy therefore combines an operating mining business with a substantial asset inventory. Both components are sensitive to the cryptocurrency’s price. Tokens generated through mining may be held rather than sold to cover expenses, which can expand exposure and affect cash needs. A higher coin count is not the same as higher spendable cash in the company’s bank accounts.

For related context, see our earlier report on the recent Zcash NU7 protocol upgrade.

The earnings split matters

The Block reported approximately $2.6 million of quarterly operating profit and substantially greater net income driven by unrealized increases in the value of the ZEC treasury. Valuation gains can be economically relevant, but they can also reverse without an operational change. Investors should read the quarterly income statement and cash-flow statement together. A business with rising book profits may still need external financing to buy new equipment or meet operating expenses if it is retaining mined tokens. The source of earnings determines how repeatable they are.

Network share and equipment expansion

The company says its fleet represented a material part of Zcash network hashrate at launch, while broader network competition has already changed that percentage. Management has discussed additional equipment purchases for 2027, subject to commitments and delivery. More hardware can produce more hashes, but miner returns depend on network difficulty, rewards, uptime, electricity and ZEC’s price. The most useful follow-up will compare actual production and operating cash with capital spent, rather than treating a treasury-size target as proof of long-term mining profitability.

Mining economics can shift even when a company executes its own operating plan well. As competitors add machines, a given fleet's fraction of network hashrate may fall, reducing expected token output at the same energy cost. Rewards also depend on protocol rules and equipment performance, while treasury purchasing introduces separate exposure to spot prices. Reporting those risks alongside current revenue helps readers understand why one profitable early period does not establish a permanent advantage. A full-year record will offer a stronger measure of the fleet's competitiveness.

For related context, see our earlier report on Bitcoin mining-difficulty changes.

Cypherpunk now has measurable mining output as well as a sizable ZEC balance. The challenge for investors is to value those as two connected but distinct businesses, avoiding the temptation to treat unrealized token appreciation as recurring operational income.

Reporting sources: Cypherpunk Q3 financial results, SEC exhibit · The Block coverage

title: DeFi Development Adds 9,482 SOL as Treasury Grows for Tenth Straight Week
description: DeFi Development Corp. has reported another increase in its Solana treasury, adding 9,482 SOL and SOL equivalents to reach approximately 2.62 million. The November 16.
fullContent:
TL;DR

  • DeFi Development disclosed 9,482 additional SOL and equivalents, taking holdings to about 2.62 million.
  • Management says its treasury has grown for ten consecutive weeks.
  • CHAD’s reported annualized preferred rate and dividend streak are separate from SOL price performance.

DeFi Development Corp. has reported another increase in its Solana treasury, adding 9,482 SOL and SOL equivalents to reach approximately 2.62 million. The November 16 SEC-filed statement describes ten consecutive weeks of holdings growth and a separate streak of 31 business days of dividends on its CHAD preferred stock. The pairing illustrates how companies built around crypto treasuries increasingly operate two different propositions: directional token exposure for common shareholders and an income-oriented capital instrument with its own terms.

The new treasury count

The filing lists approximately 2,619,311 SOL and equivalents, up from 2,609,829 in its previous update. Management says the accumulation streak began in September following a return to active buying in late August. Its activities include acquisitions, staking, validator operations and other on-chain opportunities. That mix matters because not all increases in token inventory necessarily correspond to purchasing the same number of SOL on a spot exchange. A complete shareholder analysis should separate bought tokens from rewards, then compare the increase with changes in the company’s shares and outstanding claims.

What SOL per share aims to show

The company says increasing SOL per share is a strategic objective. A coin count divided by a share count can illustrate one dimension of exposure, but it does not replace net asset value, cash-flow analysis or a review of dilution. Capital raised to buy SOL may increase total tokens while changing ownership percentages. Some holdings may also be subject to staking arrangements or operational constraints. Investors should examine the definitions attached to any company-specific per-share indicator before concluding that a higher treasury automatically improves common-equity returns.

For related context, see our earlier report on Solana corporate treasury results.

CHAD dividends are a different instrument

The firm’s variable-rate Series C perpetual preferred stock, CHAD, carries a reported 14% annual dividend rate as of the update. The company says it has made payments for 31 consecutive business days. Those distributions are subject to the preferred security’s terms and declarations by the board; a stated annualized rate is not an ironclad future payment guarantee. Common stockholders and preferred investors face different risks and rights. Presenting the preferred yield as though it were a return paid by holding SOL would be inaccurate.

The limits of the treasury comparison

Solana’s price can move substantially faster than a weekly treasury increase, so a company could report more tokens while its dollar portfolio value falls. Staking rewards are also variable and bring their own operational requirements. For DeFi Development, the most informative future disclosures will combine updated token counts with cash reserves, financing costs, issuance, validator income and the amount available to common equity. The accumulation streak is a measurable development, but its investment significance depends on what the company gave up to extend it.

Treasury-company comparisons also require attention to liabilities and timing. Two firms holding similar numbers of SOL can have very different shareholder economics if one borrowed to finance purchases, has preferred dividends to meet or issued substantially more common stock. Reported SOL-per-share figures can be useful, but the numerator and denominator should be consistently defined. Investors should also distinguish income from staking from changes in SOL's market value. Neither measure on its own guarantees liquidity to support future payments or operating expenses.

For related context, see our earlier report on Solana infrastructure updates.

This update is evidence of continued SOL accumulation and preferred-dividend activity. It is not an assurance that either share class will preserve its value, and the reported yield should not be confused with a guaranteed return on the underlying cryptocurrency.

Reporting sources: DeFi Development Corp. SEC exhibit

title: Anthropic Token Sale on Binance: The Catch Behind the Price
description:
Key Takeaways A 5% xStocks fee lifts the break-even price Delivery comes at least two hours after open Oversubscription can […]
The post Anthropic Token Sale on Binance: The Catch Behind the Price appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • A 5% xStocks fee lifts the break-even price
  • Delivery comes at least two hours after open
  • Oversubscription can leave partial or zero allocations
  • ANTx tracks Anthropic without granting shareholder rights

The campaign announcement sets the application window for November 18, 2026, from 06:00 to 14:00 UTC, with a 100 USDC minimum and a 500 million USDC cap on total subscriptions.

The 70–78 USDC per token that Binance displays excludes fees and, by Binance’s own calculation, values Anthropic at roughly $1.26 trillion to $1.41 trillion. It is also only indicative. According to Binance Wallet’s campaign FAQ, the issuer and underwriters set the final offering price after the window closes, based on demand, valuation and issuance arrangements, and that price can land above or below the range.

Applicants are therefore committing an amount of money, not buying a set number of tokens. Every cost figure below starts from the final offering price, whatever it turns out to be.

A 10% Rise Is Not a 10% Return

xStocks charges a 5% partner service fee to cover operational and distribution costs, and Binance Wallet says it adds no fee of its own. Neither the announcement nor the FAQ states whether the 5% is added on top of the committed USDC or taken out of it, or whether any charge applies to funds that go unallocated.

For break-even purposes, the first question makes no difference. If the fee is added on top, a 1,000 USDC allocation costs 1,050 USDC. If it is deducted, 1,050 USDC buys 1,000 USDC worth of tokens. Either way, each token costs 5% more than the final offering price: 73.50 USDC at the bottom of the indicative range and 81.90 USDC at the top. The mechanics change how many tokens a commitment buys, not the price ANTx must reach before an applicant is level.

That fixed hurdle shrinks every gain and deepens every loss, as the scenarios below show.

If ANTx trades this far from the final offering price…

Coindoo calculation of return on cost after the 5% partner fee. Excludes network costs, trading spreads and any charge on unallocated funds.

Delivery Comes After the Opening Trade

The announcement schedules distribution for at least two hours after Nasdaq opens, with the exact time still to be confirmed and the timeline subject to change. Neither page gives a listing date. The FAQ says only that pricing is expected on November 18.

“At least two hours” sets a floor, not a delivery promise. Whatever Anthropic’s shares do in their first hours of trading, applicants have no tokens to sell into that move. Their first available exit is the price ANTx commands once it reaches their wallets, and that is the price the fee hurdle has to clear. How tokenized shares are priced relative to the underlying stock is a separate question, covered in Coindoo’s analysis of tokenized-stock pricing.

A Partial Fill Leaves Capital Waiting

Binance describes an oversubscription model: if demand exceeds what is on offer, allocations are made in proportion to each applicant’s deposit. The issuer and underwriters set the results, and Binance Wallet applies them without discretion. Full, partial and zero allocations are all possible.

How much a single wallet can commit depends on its Alpha Points. The limit is 20,000 USDC for holders with any points, 100,000 USDC above 40 points, 200,000 USDC above 100 and 500,000 USDC above 200. Trenchers Badge holders get an extra 50,000 USDC.

Until allocations are settled, committed USDC stays locked in a non-custodial smart contract. Unused funds return to the wallet automatically afterwards, but neither page says how many days that takes.

Proportional allocation creates a trap for applicants who commit more than they want to own, expecting to be scaled back. If deposits reach twice the amount on offer, a 10,000 USDC commitment fills at roughly 5,000 USDC. If demand comes in below supply, the same commitment fills in full, and the applicant holds twice the intended position. Only an amount the applicant is prepared to hold at a full fill is safe from that outcome.

READ MORE:

Grayscale Reveals ‘Compelling Entry Points’ but Data Says No

What ANTx Actually Gives You

ANTx tracks Anthropic’s share price, but holding it does not make anyone a shareholder. The FAQ states that the tokens carry no direct ownership, voting or dividend rights and no claim against Anthropic. Any dividends may instead be reinvested or paid out at redemption, net of withholding tax.

Responsibility for the token sits with Backed, the company that issues xStocks tokenized shares, or its affiliates. Binance Wallet describes itself as the interface, not the issuer, and the FAQ notes that the issuer can blacklist wallet addresses it considers in breach of laws, regulations or sanctions.

On backing, the two companies speak with different degrees of confidence. xStocks’ product description says its tokens are backed 1:1 by underlying assets held in regulated custody. Binance’s FAQ says the backing may be cash or other eligible assets rather than the shares themselves, and that the wallet neither verifies those assets nor represents that ANTx is backed 1:1. Neither statement shows that any collateral is missing. Applicants are relying on the issuer’s word, not on a check by the platform distributing the token.

Redemption is not a simple way out either. It follows the issuer’s terms and eligibility rules, can be suspended temporarily and, where available, may carry extra fees and minimum sizes. For most holders, the realistic exit is a sale on the secondary market, which needs a buyer at an acceptable price. That is also what separates ANTx from the Anthropic pre-IPO perpetual futures: the subscription delivers a token, with no margin or funding payments attached.

The Number to Check on Distribution Day

Once tokens arrive, the wallet’s transaction history holds everything needed to measure what the campaign actually cost.

Effective entry cost per token

Total USDC deducted, fees included ÷ ANTx received

Compare it with a price you can actually sell at, not Anthropic’s Nasdaq quote.

If that figure comes out above the final offering price plus 5%, the difference is a charge the campaign documents do not describe. If the price available on the secondary market sits below it, the IPO gain shown on the chart has not reached the applicant’s wallet.

title: Former Robinhood Engineer Pleads Guilty to Trading Crypto Listings Through Hyperliquid
description: A former Robinhood software engineer has pleaded guilty to using confidential information about forthcoming crypto listings to trade perpetual futures on Hyperliquid..
fullContent:
TL;DR

  • Huaisong Xiang pleaded guilty to wire fraud linked to confidential Robinhood listing plans.
  • The Justice Department says he will forfeit $125,523 and faces sentencing in February 2027.
  • The case concerns misuse of employer information, not an allegation that Hyperliquid itself committed the fraud.

A former Robinhood software engineer has pleaded guilty to using confidential information about forthcoming crypto listings to trade perpetual futures on Hyperliquid. The US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York says Huaisong Xiang agreed to forfeit $125,523 in proceeds from the scheme. The case is a useful reminder that moving a trade to a decentralized venue does not erase legal duties tied to information obtained through an employer. It is also important to describe this as a guilty plea by one defendant, not a judgment against the entire platform or everyone named in earlier proceedings.

How the scheme worked, according to prosecutors

Federal prosecutors say Xiang had access to internal plans detailing which digital assets Robinhood would add and when public announcements were expected. Between 2025 and 2026, he used that information to take positions in perpetual futures linked to those assets before listings became public. Such instruments allow a trader to speculate on price changes without buying the underlying tokens, and they can be held without a fixed expiry if funding requirements are met. The information advantage came from alleged misuse of confidential business plans, not from a flaw in the exchange’s public data feed.

A plea is not the same as an accusation

The Justice Department’s November 16 release says Xiang pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud before US District Judge Colleen McMahon. He agreed to forfeit the stated proceeds, and sentencing is scheduled for February 25, 2027. The offense carries a statutory maximum of 20 years, but that is not a forecast of what sentence the judge will impose. This reporting describes the admitted conduct as set out by prosecutors and the plea. Any allegations against another individual should remain separate unless they are themselves resolved by court action.

For related context, see our earlier report on Hyperliquid trading and open-interest trends.

Why on-chain execution is not a legal loophole

Hyperliquid is a decentralized venue for perpetual derivatives, but the duties at the center of the case arose when confidential employer information was misappropriated. An employee’s ability to execute a trade without a conventional broker does not make the information public or remove obligations to protect it. On-chain settlement can also leave a detailed transaction trail, although linking wallets to specific people requires evidence. The case illustrates why compliance policies must cover external crypto platforms and derivatives, rather than only the trading accounts an employer officially monitors.

Implications for listing teams and traders

Companies planning token listings need clear access controls, internal approval records and policies that explain what staff may trade and when. Prosecutors’ earlier account described employees with access to nonpublic listing communications. Decentralized markets give informed actors new instruments, but do not change the underlying conflict between privileged information and fair market access. For traders, the case is not an argument that every price move before a listing is illicit; proof of confidential access, duties and misuse is the key distinction.

For compliance departments, the case illustrates why handling confidential listing plans resembles handling other market-sensitive corporate information, even when the resulting trade takes place on a decentralized venue. Firms may need clearer access controls, monitoring of employees' external accounts and written policies on information obtained through employment. Trading venues can publish transactions, but linking a wallet to the person who controls it often requires additional evidence. Regulators and prosecutors will continue to evaluate conduct under the applicable statutes rather than using blockchain transparency as an exemption.

For related context, see our earlier report on an earlier crypto-asset security case.

The plea adds a concrete enforcement example to a debate often framed in abstract terms. It shows how traditional fraud theories can reach misconduct involving on-chain perpetuals while leaving the status of ordinary public-information trading to be assessed on its own facts.

Reporting sources: US Justice Department November 16 statement

Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

title: Lighter Reopens Withdrawals After Nonce-Reuse Error Exposes Trader API Keys
description: Decentralized derivatives venue Lighter says deposits and withdrawals have resumed following a November 16 security incident that initially froze access. The latest.
fullContent:
TL;DR

  • Lighter says deposits and withdrawals have resumed after its November 16 incident.
  • Bitquery observed a roughly $10.4 million USDC withdrawal; the venue reports about $5 million returned to traders.
  • The reported root cause involved nonce reuse in unofficial signing code, not a confirmed smart-contract exploit.

Decentralized derivatives venue Lighter says deposits and withdrawals have resumed following a November 16 security incident that initially froze access. The latest explanation points to unsafe signing code used by affected trader accounts, not an announced compromise of the protocol’s smart contracts. That distinction is central to the incident: a cryptographic error in an external trading integration can expose account authority even when a venue’s core software behaves as designed.

The on-chain withdrawal was substantial

Blockchain analytics firm Bitquery traced a withdrawal of 10,393,057 USDC from a Lighter-related Ethereum contract on November 16. The funds were converted into ether, and investigators followed part of the subsequent movement through multiple wallets. Those observations establish a visible transfer trail, but they are not the same thing as a complete, audited final-loss figure. Earlier reports also cited higher possible amounts covering more than one account, which Lighter had not confirmed at the time. The safe description is an observed approximately $10.4 million USDC outflow and an incident whose recovery accounting may evolve.

Why nonce reuse can reveal a key

According to Lighter’s reported postmortem, some affected accounts used unofficial or custom signing code that reused one-time cryptographic values, known as nonces. Reusing these values with the wrong signature scheme can allow an attacker to derive secret signing material from information that was supposed to be public. Once an API signing key is compromised, apparently authorized instructions can be sent through normal account capabilities. This is not a conventional stolen-password story, and it underscores why teams should use well-tested official signing libraries rather than copy cryptographic routines into trading bots.

For related context, see our earlier report on the Unocoin wallet incident.

The pause and partial recovery

Lighter activated its Guardian safeguard during the incident, temporarily restricting withdrawals and related activity while its Security Council acted. The exchange says roughly $5 million USDC was returned to affected traders and that Guardian mode was subsequently deactivated. Its official announcements channel states that deposits and withdrawals are back to normal, with pending requests being processed. That $5 million figure should not be described as full recovery of the separately observed $10.4 million transfer. The remaining exposure and final accounting need a detailed reconciled report.

Security changes traders should understand

The venue says it has changed how API signatures are exposed and now requires wallet signatures for transfers into public pools. Further planned controls include IP allowlists, scoped permissions, per-key limits and monitoring for repeated nonces. For a trader using custom automation, the immediate lesson is to audit signing code, rotate uncertain keys and understand what each API credential can authorize. Smart-contract audits remain important, but they cannot substitute for secure key handling in external client software.

Nonce-reuse vulnerabilities are particularly serious because digital signatures rely on the uniqueness and secrecy of certain temporary values. If an attacker can infer a private key from flawed signatures, simply restarting a user interface or changing a password may not fix the exposed credential. The scope depends on which keys were affected and whether they could authorise actions beyond trading. Users should follow the protocol team's specific revocation and key-rotation instructions rather than assuming that reopening withdrawals means every associated security risk has ended.

For related context, see our earlier report on the Kava Lend exploit.

This is now a restoration-and-root-cause story, not simply a withdrawal-halt headline. The strongest follow-up will be a fully reconciled account of losses, recovered funds and the effectiveness of the new controls under live trading conditions.

Reporting sources: Lighter official announcements feed · Bitquery transaction investigation · CoinDesk initial incident coverage

Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

title: Bitmine Adds 7,653 ETH as Ethereum Treasury Climbs Above 6.08 Million Tokens
description: Ethereum treasury company Bitmine says it added 7,653 ETH over the past week, taking its reported holdings to approximately 6.08 million tokens. That is an increase in.
fullContent:
TL;DR

  • Bitmine reported ETH holdings of about 6.08 million after adding 7,653 tokens.
  • The treasury’s dollar valuation fell as the broader Ethereum market weakened.
  • Staking and accumulation strategies do not remove price, operational or financing risks.

Ethereum treasury company Bitmine says it added 7,653 ETH over the past week, taking its reported holdings to approximately 6.08 million tokens. That is an increase in the unit count, but not a guarantee that the dollar value of the position grew at the same time. Ether has been under heavy selling pressure, and the company’s reported combined crypto, cash and marketable securities holdings were worth about $11.8 billion in its November 16 update. The contrast highlights the risks of evaluating a digital-asset treasury through a single metric.

The acquisition amid a sell-off

Bitmine’s investor-relations page lists a November 16 release reporting an ETH holding above 6.08 million. The Block says the latest weekly addition was 7,653 ETH, while ether prices had declined sharply. Buying more tokens increases the number held, but changes in the price can overwhelm the value of incremental purchases over a short period. Treasury investors should therefore track both coins and fair-market value. It is possible for a company to accumulate strategically while shareholders experience a substantial decline in the marked value of the underlying asset.

The five-percent goal has consequences

Bitmine has framed its strategy around acquiring a material share of Ethereum’s circulating supply and building associated staking infrastructure. The larger the treasury becomes, the more its exposure concentrates in a single volatile asset. The company’s long-term thesis may connect ETH ownership with network activity and institutional tokenization, but that remains an investment view rather than a guaranteed economic result. Significant purchases also raise questions about how they are financed and how much incremental exposure existing shareholders receive after dilution or other capital-structure changes.

For related context, see our earlier report on institutional Ethereum yield-fund developments.

Staking adds activity, not a price floor

Bitmine has also discussed staking and validator operations as ways to earn rewards using Ethereum holdings. Staking can produce token-denominated revenue and contribute to network security. However, rewards vary with network conditions and do not remove the risk that ETH falls in dollar terms. Running validators involves technical, operational and potentially slashing or counterparty risks depending on the arrangement. A headline yield can obscure the difference between earning additional tokens and protecting shareholder purchasing power. Investors need transparent reporting on costs, locked assets and realized rewards.

How to judge the quarterly picture

The relevant questions include how much ETH is owned, what it cost, whether assets are encumbered, how staking contributes to cash or token income, and which claims sit ahead of common equity. Short-term market capitalization or portfolio value can fluctuate far more quickly than business operations change. The reported weekly purchase shows continued accumulation, while price declines mean the company’s valuation remains highly sensitive to ether markets. Watching both acquisition activity and funding terms will be more informative than treating chairman Tom Lee’s commentary as a price signal.

The key measure for an ETH treasury is not the gross holding figure alone. Issuance of new equity, financing costs, staking restrictions and any pledges against assets can change what existing shareholders effectively own. A company that buys more tokens while heavily diluting its share count may not increase exposure on a per-share basis. Conversely, a disciplined allocation can be valuable even during a short-term price decline. Quarterly cash-flow and capital-structure details will reveal more about sustainability than a single announcement of token purchases.

For related context, see our earlier report on digital-dollar liquidity trends.

Bitmine’s ETH count has risen, but the company is not insulated from the asset’s drawdown. The next disclosures should be read across holdings, financing, staking operations and balance-sheet value rather than as a contest to accumulate the largest possible token count.

Reporting sources: Bitmine investor-relations announcements · The Block report
